Pre-Registration and the Pre-Analysis Plan

Session 7

2026-10-13

Fix the analysis before the data exist

  • A p-value or a 95% interval describes a procedure: what would happen if the study ran again.
  • That procedure has to exist before the data do.
    • Chosen afterwards, it reflects the data you happened to get.
  • Deployment is the rerun that matters: real users, on the real task.
  • A pre-analysis plan (PAP) writes the procedure down and files it publicly with a timestamp.
  • It also records what everyone involved agreed to study and report.

Your PAP is the procedure your final report’s numbers describe.

Why pre-registration exists

Why write the analysis down first?

Many published findings shrink or vanish when someone checks them again.

  • Which results never reach print?
  • Does the answer depend on who analyzes the data?
  • Can an honest analyst still fool themselves?

Null results go in the file drawer

  • Franco et al.: 221 survey experiments run through TESS, a shared NSF-funded platform.
    • Every study was fielded, so the full population of results is known.
  • Strong results were 40 points more likely to be published than null results.
  • They were 60 points more likely to be written up at all.
  • Each published estimate can be honest. The published record still overstates effects.
  • A registry makes the denominator visible: every study that was started.

Franco, Malhotra & Simonovits (2014), Publication Bias in the Social Sciences: Unlocking the File Drawer, Science 345(6203).

Same data, different answers

  • Huntington-Klein et al.: 146 teams estimated the effect of DACA on full-time work three times, with more fixed each time.
  • Task 2 spread wider than Task 1 because teams did not follow the shared design exactly.

  • The analyst’s choices are a source of variation that no standard error counts.

Huntington-Klein, Portner, McCarthy & The Many Economists Collaborative on Researcher Variation (2025), The Sources of Researcher Variation in Economics, NBER WP 33729; forthcoming in JEL. Adapted from Figure 1: each team’s estimate, box = interquartile range in points.

Medicine registered trials first

  • Selectively published drug trials led to:
    • 2000: ClinicalTrials.gov opens.
    • 2005: ICMJE journals require registration before enrollment.
    • 2007: FDAAA makes registration and results reporting law in the US.
  • Kaplan & Irvin: large NHLBI trials, 1970–2012. From 2000 the primary outcome had to be registered.
  • 2012–13: Casey, Glennerster & Miguel bring PAPs to economics. The AEA and EGAP registries open.

Kaplan & Irvin (2015), Likelihood of Null Effects of Large NHLBI Clinical Trials Has Increased over Time, PLoS ONE 10(8).

Casey, Glennerster & Miguel (2012), Reshaping Institutions: Evidence on Aid Impacts Using a Preanalysis Plan, QJE 127(4).

One honest analyst can still find false positives

  • Simmons et al.: simulated studies with no true effect, and four choices left open:
    • which of two correlated outcomes to report
    • whether to add 10 subjects per condition after a first test
    • whether to control for gender or its interaction with treatment
    • whether to drop one of three conditions.
  • Making these choices after seeing the data raises the nominal 5% false-positive rate to 61%.
  • Gelman & Loken: the analyst can run just one test and still inflate it.
    • A different sample would have led to a different, equally reasonable test.
    • They call this the garden of forking paths.

A plan fixes the test before the data arrive, so the reported p-value means what it claims.

Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011), False-Positive Psychology, Psychological Science 22(11).

Gelman & Loken (2014), The Statistical Crisis in Science, American Scientist 102(6).

Forking paths in AI evaluation

  • An AI evaluator has many easy-to-try forks in the path:
    • the prompt template and system prompt
    • random seeds and the number of runs
    • temperature and other decoding settings
    • the judge model, its prompt, and its rubric
    • which questions or topics count
    • which model snapshot to compare against.
  • Singh et al.: Chatbot Arena let providers test variants privately and publish only the best.
    • Meta tested 27 private variants before the Llama 4 release.
    • The public score is the maximum of many noisy draws.

Singh et al. (2025), The Leaderboard Illusion, arXiv:2504.20879.

Summary: why pre-registration exists

  • Franco et al.: null results go unpublished. A registry shows every study started.
  • Huntington-Klein et al.: analysts disagree by more than their standard errors.
  • Simmons et al., Gelman & Loken: flexible analysis turns 5% false positives into 61%, with no fishing needed.
  • Singh et al.: a published Arena score is the best of many private variants.

Uncertainty assumes a fixed procedure

What does a 95% interval promise?

Every error bar promises something about what a rerun of the study would show.

  • Does that promise survive choosing the analysis after seeing the results?
  • What does it mean once the system is deployed?
  • How can you explore freely and still keep it?

Coverage is a property of the whole procedure

  • Lecture 06: a data set \(D\) comes from the design; an interval \(\operatorname{CI}(D)\) is a fixed function of it.

\[\text{coverage}=\Pr_{D}\big(\tau\in\operatorname{CI}(D)\big).\]

  • The probability is over reruns of the design. The function \(\operatorname{CI}\) stays the same in every rerun.
  • Now try \(k\) defensible analyses \(j=1,\dots,k\) and report the one with the smallest p-value:

\[\hat\jmath(D)=\arg\min_{j}\,p_j(D),\qquad \text{reported interval}=\operatorname{CI}_{\hat\jmath(D)}(D).\]

  • The choice of analysis now depends on \(D\). Each \(\operatorname{CI}_j\) covers 95%; the reported one covers less.
  • If the \(k\) tests were independent and \(\tau=0\): \(\Pr\big(\min_j p_j<0.05\big)=1-0.95^k\).

Simulation: reporting the best of k analyses

  • Running example (lecture 06): an LLM tutor answers 100 course questions. Retrieval over course materials is switched on for a random 50.
  • Each answer is scored 0–100. Questions vary in difficulty, a pretest predicts it, and they fall into 4 topics.
  • 16 analyses: 4 covariate sets (none, pretest, topic, both) × all questions or one topic dropped.
  • Every analysis is unbiased on its own. Picking the best of 16 gives 18% false positives and 89% coverage, and inflates the effect from 3 to 4.3 points.

Reporting the largest estimate biases it

  • The problem reaches past intervals that fail to cover.
  • Take \(k\) independent estimates of one effect, each unbiased: \(\operatorname{E}[\hat\tau_j]=\tau\).
  • An evaluator who hopes for a large effect reports the largest one:

\[\operatorname{E}\big[\max_j\hat\tau_j\big]>\tau.\]

  • With normal estimates and standard error \(s\): \(\operatorname{E}[\max_j\hat\tau_j]=\tau+c_k\,s\).
    • \(c_k\) is the expected maximum of \(k\) standard normals: \(c_2=0.56\), \(c_4=1.03\), \(c_{16}=1.77\), \(c_{27}=2.00\).
  • Hoping for a small number (error rate, cost, latency) and reporting the minimum biases it downward by the same amount.
  • If Meta’s 27 private Arena variants were equally good, the published best would sit about 2 standard errors above all of them.

Deployment is the rerun that matters

  • Lecture 06, Recht: a benchmark’s questions are fixed, so its error bar describes an imagined resampling.
    • For a benchmark run as a shared competition, that critique holds.
  • Good evaluations informs a deployment decision
    • With new users, new questions, and new runs: a fresh draw.
  • An analysis picked for its result fits the noise in this draw.
    • Deployment brings new noise, and performance falls back toward \(\tau\).
    • The expected drop is the selection bias from the previous slide.
  • Pre-registration fixes the procedure,: the reported interval describes the fresh draw.
    • How close does the evaluation’s questions and users match deployment’s?
  • A holdout on the leaderboard is better than nothing (e.g. Kaggle private holdouts)
    • Stops direct selection on outcomes, but still admits forking paths

Recht (2025), Standard error of what now?, arg min.

A written plan defines the rerun

  • A specified procedure is something another team can run again and compare.
  • Model-only evaluations are cheap to rerun. Use that:
  1. Explore on a development split: a set of seeds, a subset of questions, a pilot.
    • Try prompts, judges, and estimators freely.
  2. Write the PAP from what you learned. Fix one analysis.
  3. Confirm on a fresh run: new seeds, held-out questions, the registered analysis.
  • The exploration is reported too, labeled as exploratory.
  • Only the confirmation run carries the 95% guarantee.

Summary: uncertainty assumes a fixed procedure

  • Coverage belongs to a procedure fixed before \(D\). Choosing \(\hat\jmath(D)\) after seeing \(D\) breaks it.
  • Best of 16 in the running example: 18% false positives, 89% coverage.
  • Reporting \(\max_j\hat\tau_j\) overstates \(\tau\) by \(c_k\,s\).
  • Deployment is a fresh draw, so a selected result falls back toward \(\tau\).
  • A written plan can be rerun: explore, register, then confirm on fresh data.

What goes in a pre-analysis plan

What does a plan contain?

A plan is a document several people sign, and the final report is checked against it.

  • What has to be written down?
  • How can you test a plan before any data exist?
  • What happens when the study departs from it?

A plan is also an agreement

  • When parties with different interests evaluate together, the plan is their contract, signed before anyone knows the result.
  • US2020: Meta and outside academics ran a set of experiments on Facebook and Instagram around the 2020 US election.
    • Each plan defined the constructs in advance, such as polarization and political knowledge.
    • It also fixed the measure of each construct and the test applied to it.
    • Where the two sides disagreed on a definition, they rewrote it until both could sign.
  • The same contract settles disputes in AI evaluation:
    • Vendor and buyer: which tasks, which baseline, and what score counts as passing.
    • Lab and regulator: which harms are measured, and the threshold for release.
    • Developer and outside auditor: which snapshot, what access, and what gets published.

Dimmery (2025), What was US2020?, ddimmery.com.

MIDA: a PAP declares the whole design

  • Model: how the data arise.
    • Difficulty varies (SD 8).
    • Runs are noisy (SD 6).
    • A pretest predicts difficulty.
  • Inquiry: what you want to learn.
    • Average effect of retrieval.
    • On the 0–100 score.
    • Over these 100 questions.
  • Data strategy: how data are collected.
    • 100 questions.
    • Retrieval for 50, complete random.
    • One run each.
  • Answer strategy: how data become an answer.
    • Lin estimator with the pretest.
    • HC2 standard error.
    • 95% interval.

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, Princeton University Press, ch. 21.

Declare the design in code

design <-
  declare_model(N = 100, pretest = rnorm(N), e = rnorm(N, sd = 6),
                a = 8 * (sqrt(.6) * pretest + sqrt(.4) * rnorm(N)),
                potential_outcomes(Y ~ 50 + a + e + 3 * Z)) +
  declare_inquiry(ATE = mean(Y_Z_1 - Y_Z_0)) +
  declare_assignment(Z = complete_ra(N)) +
  declare_measurement(Y = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z)) +
  declare_estimator(Y ~ Z, covariates = ~ pretest, .method = lm_lin,
                    inquiry = "ATE", label = "Lin, pretest") +
  declare_estimator(Y ~ Z, .method = difference_in_means,
                    inquiry = "ATE", label = "Difference in means")
  • Each declare_ step is one MIDA element. The model encodes your assumptions about how the study will go.
  • The design object can draw fake data from those assumptions and run the registered estimators on it.

The mock analysis is your results section

  • run_design(design) draws one data set from your assumptions and runs the registered analysis. The output is the table and figure the paper will print.
Table 1. Effect of retrieval (simulated data)
Estimator Estimate SE CI
Lin, pretest 1.6 1.4 [-1.1, 4.4]
Difference in means 0.7 1.8 [-2.8, 4.2]
  • With the real data, only the input changes. Every reporting decision is made now.
  • If the mock figure cannot answer your research question, the real one cannot either.

Diagnosis: the mock, repeated

  • diagnose_design(design) reruns the mock on 1,000 simulated data sets.
Estimator Power Bias Coverage
Difference in means 0.30 -0.03 0.94
Lin, pretest 0.45 -0.02 0.95
  • Power says whether the sample can detect the effect you assumed.
    • Use this to calibrate your expectations and your design!
  • Bias and coverage check that the estimator and interval do what the PAP claims.

Plans change: amendments, deviations, and SOPs

  • A PAP records when each decision was made. Later learning is allowed, and labeled as such.
  • Before outcome data: file a time-stamped amendment.
  • After outcome data: run the registered analysis, then report the deviation and the reason.
    • The provider retires your pinned model snapshot mid-study.
    • The judge fails on a class of answers you did not foresee.
  • Lin & Green: a standard operating procedure (SOP) sets defaults for situations the PAP did not address.
    • The PAP overrides the SOP.
    • The Green Lab SOP is a public example you can adopt by reference.

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, Princeton University Press, chs. 21–22.

Lin & Green (2016), Standard Operating Procedures: A Safety Net for Pre-Analysis Plans, PS: Political Science & Politics 49(3).

After the data: populated PAP and reconciliation

  • Populated PAP: run the registered code on the real data. Each mock table gets its real numbers.
  • Reconciliation: list every place the analysis departs from the plan.
    • Inquiry: each registered estimand, and whether the report answers it.
    • Answer strategy: each planned estimator next to the one reported, with the reason for any change.
  • Report both estimates when they differ. The reader decides how much the change matters.
    • Generally keep the complete results in the appendix

Your reconciliation tables become the final report’s “deviations and surprises” section.

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, Princeton University Press, ch. 22.

Summary: what goes in a pre-analysis plan

  • A PAP is a public, time-stamped agreement. Contested definitions are settled before anyone knows which answer they favor.
  • It declares the whole design: Model, Inquiry, Data strategy, Answer strategy.
  • run_design produces the mock tables and figures. diagnose_design reports power, bias, and coverage for each registered estimator.
  • Amend before outcome data, document deviations after, and let an SOP cover the unforeseen. The reconciliation tables report every departure.

Writing your PAP, step by step

From a design to a registered plan

Your team now writes its own plan and registers it on OSF by Friday 30 October.

  • What goes in each step?
  • How specific is specific enough?

Ten steps, four graded components

Constructs

  • 1. Research question
  • 3. Construct, outcome, and scoring

Research design

  • 2. Frozen instrument
  • 4. Sampling, sample size, randomization
  • 8. Threats to validity and defenses

Analysis plan

  • 5. Hypotheses
  • 6. Estimator, covariates, standard error
  • 7. Missing data, non-compliance, many tests

Process

  • 9. Mock analysis in a literate notebook
  • 10. Registration and deviation protocol
  • Work through the steps in numerical order. Each component is worth 5 of the 20 points.

Constructs: question, construct, and scoring

  • Step 1, research question: one sentence naming the system, the comparison, and the population.
    • Does retrieval over course materials improve tutor answers to questions students in this course ask?
  • Step 3, construct and scoring:
    • the construct (answer quality) and why the outcome captures it
    • the scoring rule: rubric, scale, and who or what applies it
    • the judge’s validation against human labels (lecture 04), with its agreement statistic
    • the human-labeled sample used to correct the judge (lecture 06).
  • These steps declare the model and the inquiry.

Research design: instrument, sample, assignment, threats

  • Step 2, frozen instrument:
    • model snapshot ids, with the date each was pinned
    • the prompting approach and decoding settings
    • how versions will be recorded when the study runs.
  • Step 4, sampling and assignment:
    • the question population and how questions are drawn from it
    • sample size from a power calculation
    • the randomization: unit, blocks, and how the seed is fixed.
  • Step 8, threats: threats from the course, paired with a defense.
    • Contamination: benchmark questions may be in the training data. Defense: write 40 new questions after the model’s cutoff.
  • These steps declare the data strategy.

Analysis plan: hypotheses, estimator, missing data, many tests

  • Step 5, hypotheses: one primary hypothesis tied to one estimand. Secondary hypotheses are listed and labeled.
  • Step 6, estimation:
    • the estimator, with covariates named
    • the standard error and its clustering level
    • the interval, and its small-sample version if needed.
  • Step 7, the unplanned:
    • a fixed rule for refusals, API errors, and users who stop
    • the retry policy
    • the correction for multiple tests: Holm or Benjamini–Hochberg.
  • These steps declare the answer strategy.

Process: mock analysis, registration, deviations

  • Step 9, mock analysis: a literate notebook that simulates data from your model and produces every planned table and figure.
    • Report power, bias, and coverage from the same simulation.
  • Step 10, registration:
    • register on OSF by Friday 30 October
    • attach a frozen snapshot of the repository: PAP, harness, analysis code
    • state the deviation protocol: amendments before data, documented deviations after.
  • Process on GitHub: the PAP steward breaks the plan into issues, assigns them, and reviews the pull requests.

Vague versus specific

Vague

  • We will compare the accuracy of the two Bundles and test whether the difference is significant.
  • We will control for relevant covariates.
  • We will handle missing data appropriately.

Specific

  • Estimand: mean score with retrieval minus without, over the 200 sampled questions.
  • Estimator: Lin, covariates pilot difficulty and topic. CR2 SE clustered on question (5 runs each); \(t\) interval.
  • Test: two-sided, \(\alpha=0.05\).
  • Missing: a refusal or failed call after 3 retries scores 0, analyzed as assigned. Missingness reported by arm.
  • Test each item: could two teams follow it independently and get the same number?

Summary: writing your PAP

  • Steps 1 and 3 declare the model and inquiry. Steps 2, 4, and 8 declare the data strategy. Steps 5–7 declare the answer strategy.
  • Step 9’s mock notebook produces every planned table and figure, with power, bias, and coverage.
  • Step 10 registers the PAP and a frozen repository snapshot on OSF by Friday 30 October.
  • An item is specific enough when two teams could follow it independently and get the same number.
